screens.title: Embedded Software for Soft-Core Processors
screens.subtitle: Writing, building, and debugging C software for NIOS II using the BSP, HAL, and JTAG.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how to take a Qsys hardware system and make it useful by writing embedded software that runs on the NIOS II soft-core. We focus on the NIOS II Software Build Tools for Eclipse: how to create a software project, generate the Board Support Package that describes your hardware, and use the HAL A P I so your code can talk to UART, GPIO, and timers without hardcoded addresses. You will also see how the IOWR and IORD macros use base address symbols from system. h, why the linker script matters for where code and data live, and how to use the JTAG debugger to step through code and inspect variables. A concrete example—blinking LEDs and reading a pushbutton—ties these pieces together so you see code, generated headers, and the live FPGA behavior at once. By the end you’ll understand how hardware and software relate, how BSP regeneration preserves portability as hardware changes, and how JTAG helps diagnose timing or register issues. Consider how treating hardware as a set of abstracted APIs reduces errors and speeds iteration when you modify a Qsys design.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: The BSP and HAL make your NIOS II software portable and readable by mapping hardware into a C API; JTAG debugging and the linker script let you test and place code correctly on the FPGA.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Tools and Skills
screens.subtitle: What you should be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus on practical skills you will use while developing embedded software for the NIOS II processor. First, you will learn to write, compile, and debug C programs using the NIOS II Software Build Tools for Eclipse. This matters because the SBT integrates compilation, linker use, and the JTAG debugger so you can move quickly from code to on-FPGA execution. Second, you will understand the Board Support Package: what files it contains, how the HAL provides portable peripheral access, and why regenerating the BSP after hardware changes is essential. Third, you will be able to use the HAL A P I to access UART, GPIO, and a timer; this means using high-level functions and macros rather than hardcoded addresses to avoid brittle code. Finally, you will learn to download and run software on the FPGA and use the JTAG debugger to set breakpoints, step code, and inspect variables. Each skill reduces integration friction and prevents common mistakes such as mismatched base addresses or placing data in the wrong memory region. Practice these objectives with a blink-and-button lab to cement the workflow and confidence.

keyIdea.title: Practical focus
keyIdea.text: Learn SBT for Eclipse, BSP generation, HAL-based peripheral access, and JTAG debugging so software and hardware work together smoothly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical outcomes
screens.subtitle: How these skills fit into real FPGA projects

narration.text: These objectives place the skills into practical contexts you will meet in a capstone project. Writing and debugging with the NIOS II SBT lets you attach a processor to custom logic and test algorithm behavior on real input and output. Understanding the BSP prevents the common pitfall of hardcoding addresses; instead, the BSP generates system. h and linker scripts that match your hardware configuration. Using the HAL A P I, especially macros for peripheral access, means your code will run with different Qsys topologies without change. Downloading code and using the JTAG debugger gives you a way to pause the processor and inspect the state of variables and registers, which is critical when timing or peripheral initialization does not behave as expected. A concrete use case is adding a pushbutton GPIO: you will regenerate the BSP, recompile software, and use a breakpoint while the button handler runs to confirm the GPIO register reads the expected value. These skills shorten integration cycles and reduce subtle bugs when combining HDL and C code.

screens.title: The Board Support Package (BSP)
screens.subtitle: What the BSP contains and why it matters

narration.text: Start by understanding the Board Support Package, or BSP, because it is the bridge between your Qsys hardware design and your C application. The BSP is generated from the Qsys system file and contains several things: the HAL that provides C functions for peripherals, a newlib port for common C library routines, device drivers specific to the peripherals in your system, linker scripts that map code and data to memories, and system header files that define base address macros for every component. Why this matters: without the BSP you would have to hand-code base addresses and register layouts, which causes errors and makes code non-portable when you add or remove peripherals. A concrete example is the PIO LED peripheral: its base address appears as PIO_LED_BASE in system. h. The HAL macros such as IOWR_ALTERA_AVALON_PIO_DATA use that symbol to write the LED register. A common misconception is that the BSP is optional or only for drivers — in practice it is essential because the linker script and headers are matched to the hardware mapping. Always regenerate the BSP after changing Qsys so headers and linker settings stay correct. Key takeaway: treat the BSP as an auto-generated contract between hardware and software.

keyIdea.title: BSP role
keyIdea.text: BSP packages HAL, drivers, newlib, headers, and linker scripts to map software to hardware consistently.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › BSP
Core Concept

Board Support Package

A generated collection of headers, drivers, HAL, newlib, and linker scripts that match your Qsys system.
HAL
C functions and macros to access UART, GPIO, timers without raw addresses.
Device drivers
Peripheral-specific code produced for the components present in Qsys.
Linker script
Defines memory regions for code and data based on on-chip memory or external SDRAM.
system.h
Generated header with base address macros like PIO_LED_BASE used by HAL macros.
Practical example: LED PIO
/* system.h contains: */
#define PIO_LED_BASE 0x00001000

/* HAL write uses the base symbol: */
IOWR_ALTERA_AVALON_PIO_DATA(PIO_LED_BASE, 0xFF);
Regenerate BSP
When you add or remove peripherals in Qsys, regenerate the BSP so system.h and the linker script remain correct for your software build.
Key Takeaway
Treat the BSP as the authoritative mapping of hardware to software interfaces; it prevents hardcoded-address bugs.

screens.title: HAL API and Register Macros
screens.subtitle: How IOWR and IORD, and base macros in system.h make code portable

narration.text: The HAL, or Hardware Abstraction Layer, provides the set of functions and macros you call from C to control peripheral hardware on the NIOS II. Two central primitives are the macros that read and write peripheral registers: IOWR and IORD. These macros take a base address symbol such as PIO_LED_BASE and a data value or register offset, so the application code never hardcodes numeric addresses. The base symbols are found in system. h, which is generated by the BSP and matches the Qsys mapping. For example, writing to LEDs is simply a macro call that uses the symbol PIO_LED_BASE; if you move the LED peripheral to a different address in Qsys later, regenerating the BSP updates system. h and your code continues to compile and run. A common mistake is to assume registers are stable across designs and to paste literal addresses into code. That approach breaks portability and confuses debugging. A small concrete example: reading a timer status with IORD_ALTERA_AVALON_TIMER_STATUS(TIMER_BASE) returns the timer register using the symbol TIMER_BASE from system. h. Key takeaway: always use the HAL macros and generated base symbols to keep code portable across Qsys changes.

keyIdea.title: HAL abstraction
keyIdea.text: IOWR/IORD and base macros in system.h remove address-level dependencies so code stays portable when hardware changes.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › HAL API
Definition

IOWR and IORD macros

Macros provided by the HAL that wrap reads and writes to peripheral registers using generated base address symbols.

IOWR_ALTERA_AVALON_PIO_DATA(PIO_LED_BASE, value); // write LED data
alt_u32 status = IORD_ALTERA_AVALON_TIMER_STATUS(TIMER_BASE); // read timer
Misconception: using literal addresses seems faster but produces brittle code. The HAL macros are compiler-friendly and portable when BSP regenerates system.h.
Practical mapping
system.h
Contains macros like PIO_LED_BASE defined to the peripheral's base address assigned by Qsys.
#include "system.h"

/* use generated base symbol, not a literal */
IOWR_ALTERA_AVALON_PIO_DATA(PIO_LED_BASE, 0xFF);
Quick Check
If you move a peripheral in Qsys and forget to regenerate the BSP, compilation may still succeed but runtime reads/writes target the wrong address. Regenerate BSP and rebuild.

screens.title: Blink LED — Code Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A minimal NIOS II C program and how HAL is used

narration.text: Let's walk through a small but important example: a blink program that produces a chasing LED pattern. This sample shows how to include generated headers, write to a PIO peripheral via HAL macros, and use the provided usleep function to create delays. The program starts by setting an initial pattern and then loops: writing the pattern with the write macro, sleeping for half a second, and shifting the pattern. An important detail is that usleep is provided by the BSP newlib/HAL integration so calling it uses the system timer implementation. The code relies on PIO_LED_BASE from system. h, keeping hardware addresses out of the application. A common misconception is that delays are always precise; in embedded systems, usleep timing depends on the timer configuration and clock settings from the hardware side. When you debug this code with JTAG, you can set a breakpoint inside the loop to inspect the led_pattern variable and confirm the write macro updates the PIO register. This walkthrough links the visible code lines to the generated BSP elements so you understand where headers, macros, and timing come from.

keyIdea.title: Example insight
keyIdea.text: The blink program shows how generated headers, HAL macros, and BSP-provided time functions work together to make simple hardware control reliable.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › Blink Example
Code Walkthrough
Blink LED
#include <unistd.h>
#include "system.h"
#include "altera_avalon_pio_regs.h"

int main(void) {
  alt_u32 led_pattern = 0x01;

  while (1) {
    IOWR_ALTERA_AVALON_PIO_DATA(PIO_LED_BASE, led_pattern);
    usleep(500000);  /* 500 ms */

    led_pattern = led_pattern << 1;
    if (led_pattern == 0)
      led_pattern = 0x01;
  }
  return 0;
}
Annotations
  • Include system.h: supplies PIO_LED_BASE, TIMER_BASE and other base address macros generated by the BSP.
  • IOWR macro: writes a value to the LED PIO register using the HAL-provided macro.
  • usleep: provided by the BSP/newlib integration and uses the system timer implementation.
  • Pattern logic: shifting and wrap-around produce a chasing LED effect; inspect led_pattern with JTAG to verify behavior.
Key Takeaway

This simple program demonstrates how BSP headers, HAL macros, and timer functions integrate to control hardware without magic addresses.

screens.title: Creating and Regenerating the BSP
screens.subtitle: From Qsys system file to a usable software project

narration.text: Creating the Board Support Package is a short process but it must be repeated whenever your hardware design changes. The usual flow begins in Qsys: you add or configure peripherals and generate the system file. Then in the NIOS II SBT you create a new software project and choose to generate a BSP for the system—this produces system. h, device drivers, HAL sources, and the linker script. If you later add a new peripheral, for example a pushbutton GPIO, you must regenerate the BSP so the new base address and driver are visible to your C code. Regeneration updates headers and linker regions; failing to regenerate is a common source of mismatch bugs because your code will still compile against an outdated system. h or link to wrong memory regions. A practical step sequence: 1) Modify Qsys and generate a new. sopcinfo, 2) In SBT, select "Generate BSP from system description," 3) Rebuild the BSP and recompilation of your application. A misconception is that you can manually edit system. h—do not. Treat generated files as authoritative and regenerate instead of hand-editing. This disciplined flow ensures software always matches the deployed hardware mapping.

keyIdea.title: BSP lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Generate BSP from the Qsys system file and regenerate it whenever hardware changes to keep headers and linker scripts consistent.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › BSP Regeneration
Process

Generate BSP and rebuild

  1. 1. Edit Qsys: add or configure peripherals and regenerate the .sopcinfo system file.
  2. 2. Generate BSP: in NIOS II SBT choose the option to create or regenerate the BSP for the current system file.
  3. 3. Rebuild application: rebuild your C project so the compiler and linker use the updated system.h and linker script.
Tip: treat generated files as machine authoritative. Manual edits create drift between hardware and software mappings and inevitably cause runtime errors.
Example
Scenario: you add a pushbutton input PIO to Qsys. After regenerating the .sopcinfo you regenerate the BSP. The new system.h contains PIO_BUTTON_BASE. Your button-reading code uses that symbol; rebuild ensures it links correctly.
Common mistake
Not regenerating the BSP but reusing compiled object files leads to mismatched addresses and puzzling bugs at runtime.

screens.title: UART: printf via JTAG or STDOUT
screens.subtitle: How printf reaches the host or the JTAG UART

narration.text: One practical feature of the BSP and HAL integration is that standard output functions like printf are routed through the available UART interface, which may be a JTAG UART or a standard STDOUT UART depending on your project. The BSP configures which device satisfies stdout, so when you call the print function in your C code, the HAL sends characters to the selected UART device automatically. This is convenient for simple console messages, logging, and debugging without a full terminal driver. A concrete example is printing status on pushbutton events: calling the print function whenever the button is pressed lets you observe behavior in a host terminal. A misconception is expecting printf always to be instantaneous; depending on the UART and buffering, output may be delayed or require polling. Also note that the presence and name of JTAG UART depends on the Qsys design; if the design lacks a UART, printf calls will not produce visible output. In practice, confirm the BSP includes a UART device and check the Eclipse console configuration before relying on printed messages for debugging. UART: printf via JTAG or STDOUT means printf uses the bsp-selected uart device (jtag or stdout) so console output depends on the qsys configuration and bsp mappings.. In practical terms, how printf reaches the host or the jtag uart. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UART routing
keyIdea.text: printf uses the BSP-selected UART device (JTAG or STDOUT) so console output depends on the Qsys configuration and BSP mappings.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › UART & printf
Comparison

JTAG UART vs STDOUT UART

JTAG UART: connected via the JTAG debugger, convenient for development, appears in the Eclipse console.
STDOUT UART: a physical UART wired to a host serial port or USB-UART, useful for standalone operation after debugging.
Confirm which UART the BSP designates for stdout; the BSP controls routing so your print calls work as expected.
Example
In your button-lab, call the print function when a press is detected: "Button pressed!" If the JTAG UART is present, this message appears in the Eclipse console when you run the program under the debugger.
Practical note
If you see no output, check that a UART device exists in Qsys and that the BSP was regenerated after adding it. Also verify the Eclipse console is set to read the correct UART stream.

screens.title: Using the JTAG Debugger
screens.subtitle: Breakpoints, stepping, and inspecting variables on the FPGA

narration.text: Debugging embedded software on the NIOS II is practical because the processor includes a JTAG debug module. Using a USB-Blaster cable connected to the DE10-Lite board, you start the NIOS II debugger inside Eclipse and the toolchain downloads the compiled program into the FPGA's memory and runs it. You can then set breakpoints in C code, pause execution, step line-by-line, inspect variables, and view processor registers. A typical debugging workflow is to set a breakpoint inside an ISR or a button handler and press the physical button while the debugger is running to capture the exact register values at that moment. This helps verify that peripheral reads match expectations. A misconception is thinking JTAG only helps at startup; in fact, you can attach and detach, and you can pause a running system to probe runtime state. Use variable inspection to confirm types and values from device drivers and check the memory map if data appears corrupted. When stepping through hardware-interfacing code, watch for side effects: writes using IOWR will change peripheral state immediately. The final practicality is that JTAG shortens the feedback loop between code change and visible hardware effect, letting you validate both HDL and software together.

keyIdea.title: Debug power
keyIdea.text: JTAG lets you stop and inspect live processor state so you can verify register values, variable contents, and peripheral behavior during execution.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › JTAG Debugging
Steps
  1. Connect USB-Blaster: attach the cable to the DE10-Lite board and your workstation.
  2. Start debugger: use the SBT Eclipse debugger to download and run your program on the FPGA.
  3. Set breakpoints: pause execution at a code line of interest and inspect variables or memory.
  4. Step and resume: step line-by-line or resume to observe peripheral interactions in real time.
When inspecting variables, confirm types match driver expectations and watch for volatile-qualified registers which can change outside the CPU.
Example
Set a breakpoint in a button press handler. Press the hardware pushbutton and the debugger will pause at the handler so you can inspect the GPIO data register and the led_pattern variable value to confirm correct behavior.
Watchout
Remember that stepping through code changes timing; bugs that depend on precise timing may not appear when stopped and stepped, so supplement with logging via UART when needed.

screens.title: Memory Regions and the Linker Script
screens.subtitle: How the BSP maps code and data to on-chip memory or external SDRAM

narration.text: Memory management for the NIOS II uses a flat model where code, stack, heap, and data reside in defined regions. The BSP includes a linker script that assigns sections to memories available in the Qsys system. For a small project, on-chip memory suffices for program code and data. As programs grow, you may add external SDRAM in Qsys and update the linker script to place larger regions in SDRAM. The linker script is part of the BSP so it always reflects the hardware memory map. Practically, the script defines where. text,. data,. bss, heap, and stack live. A common pitfall is assuming variables will fit in on-chip memory; if you allocate large static arrays without adjusting the linker script or adding SDRAM, you will overflow memory at runtime. When you add SDRAM in Qsys, regenerate the BSP so the linker script includes SDRAM regions. Verify memory placement by inspecting the map file generated at link time and by using the debugger to check pointer addresses during execution. The key learning is that software memory layout is determined by the BSP-provided linker script and must align with your hardware memory design.

keyIdea.title: Memory mapping
keyIdea.text: The BSP linker script maps program and data sections to the memories declared in Qsys; add SDRAM and regenerate BSP when larger memory is required.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › Linker & Memory
Definition

Linker script and memory regions

The BSP supplies a linker script that assigns program and data sections to on-chip memory or external SDRAM defined in Qsys.

  • .text: program code
  • .data and .bss: initialized and zeroed data
  • heap and stack: runtime allocations and call frames
Practical advice
If your binary grows beyond on-chip memory, add SDRAM to Qsys and regenerate the BSP so the linker script can place large regions into SDRAM. Inspect the map file to confirm placements.
Common mistake

Declaring large static buffers without configuring sufficient RAM leads to runtime crashes. Check linker output and memory addresses in the debugger to confirm placement.

screens.title: Lab: Button Input and UART Message
screens.subtitle: Extend Qsys, regenerate BSP, and debug the button handler

narration.text: A practical hands-on activity ties all previous ideas together. Start by adding a pushbutton GPIO in Qsys and regenerating the. sopcinfo. In the NIOS II SBT generate the BSP so system. h includes PIO_BUTTON_BASE and the device driver. In your C application, poll or interrupt on the pushbutton GPIO; when a press is detected toggle the LED pattern and call the print function to emit "Button pressed!" to the configured UART. Use the JTAG debugger to set a breakpoint inside the button handler and press the physical button; when paused, inspect the GPIO data register to ensure it contains the expected value. This lab emphasizes the full cycle: hardware change, BSP regeneration, rebuild, program download via JTAG, and live debugging. A common issue is forgetting to regenerate the BSP after adding the button; if prints or register symbols are missing, stop and regenerate. By completing this flow you confirm that HAL macros, generated base symbols, and the JTAG debugger combine to provide a reliable development loop for embedded projects. Lab: Button Input and UART Message means add a pushbutton, regenerate bsp, and use jtag to debug the handler that toggles leds and prints a message.. In practical terms, extend qsys, regenerate bsp, and debug the button handler. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Add a pushbutton, regenerate BSP, and use JTAG to debug the handler that toggles LEDs and prints a message.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › Hands-on Activity
Steps
  1. Add a pushbutton PIO in Qsys and regenerate the system file.
  2. In NIOS II SBT, regenerate the BSP so system.h contains PIO_BUTTON_BASE.
  3. Write code to read the button and toggle led_pattern; call the print function when pressed.
  4. Download program via JTAG and use a breakpoint inside the handler to inspect the GPIO register value.
Example snippet
/* Read button and toggle */
alt_u32 btn = IORD_ALTERA_AVALON_PIO_DATA(PIO_BUTTON_BASE);
if (btn) {
  /* toggle pattern and print */
  printf("Button pressed!
");
}
Use the debugger to pause when the printf is called and verify that the button register holds the expected bit pattern.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Summary of essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts to carry forward. First, the Board Support Package is the generated contract between your Qsys hardware and the software build; it contains HAL, drivers, system headers, and the linker script. Second, use the HAL A P I including IOWR and IORD macros and the generated base symbols in system. h so your application code stays portable when the Qsys topology changes. Third, the JTAG debugger is the primary tool for live debugging on the NIOS II: it downloads your program, lets you set breakpoints, step through execution, and inspect variables and registers to confirm hardware-software interactions. Keep these three ideas in mind as you build larger projects: always regenerate BSP after hardware changes, prefer HAL macros over hardcoded addresses, and use JTAG to validate runtime behavior. A useful question to reflect on: when adding a new peripheral, what steps will you perform to ensure software and hardware stay synchronized?

keyIdea.title: Three anchors
keyIdea.text: BSP, HAL with IOWR/IORD, and JTAG debugging are the essential anchors for NIOS II embedded development.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › Key Concepts
BSP generation
Generate BSP from Qsys so headers and linker scripts match hardware.
HAL / IOWR / IORD
Use HAL macros with base symbols from system.h rather than literal addresses.
JTAG Debugging
Use the JTAG debugger to step, set breakpoints, and inspect variables on the FPGA.
Summary takeaway
Treat the BSP as authoritative, use HAL macros for portability, and rely on JTAG to validate runtime behavior between your C code and Qsys peripherals.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you build

narration.text: Before you move to the capstone, keep a quick checklist in mind. First, regenerate the BSP whenever you change hardware so system. h, drivers, and the linker script reflect the current Qsys mapping. Second, use the HAL APIs and the IOWR/IORD macros with base symbols rather than hardcoded addresses to make your code portable and readable. Third, use the JTAG debugger to step through execution and inspect variables and peripheral registers; this is the most direct way to confirm that your software and HDL interact as intended. These three reminders are the minimum discipline that prevents common integration errors and speeds iterative development. Ask yourself: after adding a new peripheral, have I regenerated the BSP, rebuilt the application, and tested it under JTAG? If the answer is yes, proceed to integrate more features confidently.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Regenerate BSP, use HAL macros, and validate with JTAG every time you change hardware or behavior.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 8.4 › Quick Reference
1 — Regenerate BSP
Keep headers and linker sections in sync with hardware.
2 — Use HAL macros
IOWR/IORD with PIO_XXX_BASE symbols, not literals.
3 — Validate with JTAG
Step, inspect, and confirm peripheral state during runtime.
Final question
After adding a new pushbutton in Qsys, what three steps ensure your software will use it correctly? Regenerate the BSP, rebuild the application, and verify with JTAG.
